newsitem.title: UK: Blair's deputy is key figure in Labour election bid.
newsitem.headline: Blair's deputy is key figure in Labour election bid.

text.p: His blunt northern accent and tortured syntax is at odds with the polished delivery of British Labour leader Tony Blair.
Often deputy party leader John Prescott seems to be a throwback to the days when union activists dominated a party of the workers.

Blair himself dazzled the minds of Labour supporters and the traditionally sceptical media with his keynote speech on Tuesday to Labour's last annual conference before the general election -- now no more than seven months away.
But it was Prescott, 58, a former cruise ship steward, who won the hearts of the delegates in this northern seaside resort on Wednesday.

A day after Blair mapped out the road to power with 10 pledges for government and the promise of a "new age of enlightenment", Prescott put the party on a war footing, urging supporters to get to work now for an election victory.
Ordering them to saturate the streets of 90 parliamentary seats which will decide whether Labour ends 17 years of Conservative rule, Prescott told them, "Enough is enough".

The rapturous reception bore testament to the affection ordinary Labour party members have for a man who left school at 15 and became active in trade unions and politics after working as a ship's steward.

But it was also a tribute to the position he has won in a party led by a man poles apart from Prescott in background and upbringing, power underlined by his role as mastermind of the opposition party's election campaign drive.

For Prescott, a rival to Blair for the leadership after the death of former leader John Smith in 1994, has forged a unique role as fixer in a party Blair has dragged from the left to the centre of the political spectrum.
The fixer role fits easily on the solid frame of the railway clerk's son.

But it has taken all his toughness to push through reforms for Blair and Smith -- a 1993 reform of party democracy and last year's ditching of a traditional party commitment to mass industrial ownership -- seen as central to Labour's new vigour.
On both occasions Prescott, despite personal misgivings, swung himself behind the leaders, winning support from unions and party members for the highly controversial reforms.

It is the fact that Prescott, who completed his education at university as a trade union-sponsored adult student, is seen as retaining the traditional socialist conscience of the pre-Blair Labour party that allowed him to pull off such appeals.
Blair may have been the man who revolutionised the party and brought it close to power. But without Prescott, such a transition would not have been hard if not impossible.
Such loyalty is recognised by Blair, who said in his conference speech: "If I'm fighting in the jungle there's nobody I'd rather have with me than John Prescott."

But the strange relationship between the sharp lawyer with deep religious convictions at the head of the party and the bluff former steward who can alternate between truculence and infectious laughter is still an enigma to most.
For Britain's media, still largely dominated by newspapers traditionally friendly to the Conservatives, it has given rise to rumour after rumour of splits and rows.
Such rumours are dismissed by Prescott, who describes his relationship with Blair as open and frank, but extremely warm and filled with respect, as mischief-making.
His loyalty has been tested, both by the pace of reform and attacks on the leader's style of leadership by friends of Prescott, and each time he has lined up behind Blair.
If Blair wins the election, as polls suggest and as commentators increasingly forecast, that loyalty will be rewarded with a key role in government.
